title: Contracts, negative tests and boundaries
goal: Choose tests by input class and distinguish a parsing fault from a range-check fault.

prerequisites.text: Inclusive bounds, parsing one line, and observing the result before and after a change.

terms.title: Input class
terms.definition: A set of inputs for which the same rule applies for the same reason.

terms.title: Boundary neighbour
terms.definition: The nearest value on one side of a boundary. Compare it with the boundary itself and the nearest value on the other side.

terms.title: Negative test
terms.definition: A check that a specific condition, such as extra text or an out-of-range number, is rejected as specified.

sections.title: One result can hide several reasons
paragraphs: A terminal accepts a daily limit from 1 through 24. The line 25 contains an integer outside the limits. The line 12x begins with an in-range number, but the full line is malformed. Both return invalid, so test both reasons separately.

Build a table with both boundaries, their nearest neighbours, an ordinary case and malformed inputs. Label the reason for each expected result so that each check covers a particular part of the contract.

sections.title: Checking a daily limit
paragraphs: strtol writes the address of the first unread character into end. read_value permits surrounding whitespace and rejects other suffixes. The comparisons against 1 and 24 happen only after parsing.
steps: Enter 24. Parsing yields 24, value > 24 is false and the program prints valid.
Enter 25. Parsing still succeeds, but the upper check is now true. The program prints invalid.
Enter 12x. After strtol, end points to x. read_value rejects the line.

sections.title: Identify the fault by its input
paragraphs: If 24 gives invalid, inspect the upper-bound operator. If 12x gives valid, inspect what remains after strtol. Different inputs expose the two defects.
The separate diagnostic snippet omits an argument, so compilation is rejected. The program has not checked any input at that point.

sections.title: Try a different pair of thresholds
paragraphs: Practice accepts 10–18. List 9, 10, 17, 18, 19 and a valid-looking prefix with a suffix. Record the expected results before comparing them with the output.

reading.author: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14
reading.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 — Programming languages — C
reading.purpose: Choose tests by input class and distinguish a parsing fault from a range-check fault.

selfcheck.prompt: Which test exposes a check of value >= 24 rather than value > 24?
feedback: 17 is in range with either check.
Only 24 distinguishes the inclusive boundary from the exclusive one.
The numeric prefix 12 is in range.
end points at x, so reject the complete line.

selfcheck.prompt: Why record the expected reason when 25 and 12x print the same result?
selfcheck.feedback: The first case checks the range after parsing. The second checks input syntax. Each result covers a different condition.

practice.title: A booking window from 10 to 18
practice.task: Accept numbers from 10 through 18. Parse the first line as a decimal integer with an optional sign and surrounding whitespace. Print valid for valid input or invalid otherwise. Fill in a table of input classes first, then fix suffix parsing and the upper boundary. Reject lines longer than 63 bytes before the newline.
criteria: 10, 18 and a number with surrounding whitespace are accepted. 9 and 19 give invalid.
12x, abc and an overflowing number give invalid. Label each distinct cause.
practice.hint: 18 and 12x expose two different faults. Find the *end check in the parser and the comparison with 18 in main.

steps.action: Record the class and expected result for 18 and 12x, then run both on the starter.
steps.why: The inputs isolate the parsing and comparison faults.
steps.expected: 18 incorrectly gives invalid, and 12x incorrectly gives valid.

steps.action: Fix the suffix check and the threshold, then rerun the boundary and negative cases.
steps.why: Each cause needs its own passing check.
steps.expected: 18 gives valid, 12x gives invalid, 9 and 19 give invalid, and 10 gives valid.

exercises.title: Independent transfer
exercises.task: In a separate copy, use 5–9 and choose six inputs before running: two boundaries, their two outer neighbours, one ordinary value and one with a suffix.
criteria: 4 and 10 give invalid; 5 and 9 give valid. 7 and 7x check distinct classes.
